blocks.content: Vertical erosion dominates during the youth stage of a river, carving steep-sided V-shaped valleys, deep gorges, and canyons.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: River erosional landforms develop predominantly during the upper or youth stage of a river where vertical incision dominates over lateral erosion.
V-shaped valleys, gorges, and canyons are formed by progressive downcutting of the river bed into hard bedrock.
Potholes are circular depressions cut into the solid rock of the riverbed through the process of abrasion and eddy currents.
Plunge pools are large, deep depressions formed at the base of waterfalls by the impact of falling water and boulders.
River terraces are elevated abandoned floodplains left behind as the river rejuvenates and cuts deeper into its valley.

rows: Equal width at top and bottom
Significantly wider at the top than at the bottom
Forms in resistant bedrock under humid or high-relief conditions
Forms in flat-lying sedimentary rocks in arid or semi-arid regions

items: Questions frequently contrast gorges (equal width at top and bottom, steep vertical walls) with canyons (wider at top than bottom, step-like slopes formed in arid environments).
Potholes and plunge pools are micro-erosional features specific to the upper/youth course of rivers.
Incised or entrenched meanders result from river rejuvenation, where an existing meandering stream restarts deep vertical downcutting.
